supported_claims.text: 爸 is read as “father” and is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 父 contributes the father meaning, while 巴 is proposed as a sound component.

The consulted research reports an early lexical record in 廣雅 glossing 爸 as father, while noting that 爸 is absent from 說文. This supports an attested use of the word, not a date or explanation for the graph’s formation.

The component-level sound analysis reports 巴 *praː and 爸 *praː in Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system. This is a proposed sound comparison; the dossier does not independently establish 巴’s original referent or name.

The father word written 爸 is also discussed as phonologically related to 父, but that is a lexical interpretation distinct from the graph’s proposed 巴 sound component. The cited forms include 父 and 爸 as *baʔ in Zhengzhang’s system; modern Mandarin has 父 fù and 爸 bà.
The curated oracle-style images are modern redraws of 父 and 巴 separately. They illustrate proposed components, not an early occurrence of the complete graph 爸.

disagreements.text: 巴’s early graphic interpretation is unsettled: the transmitted 說文 tradition links it to a giant snake, while a modern paleographic proposal interprets forms read as 巴 as a kneeling person; the dossier does not establish either as the original referent.

A historical lexicographic account proposes that an elder-father word represented by 八八 or 巴巴 was written with 父 added, while later research argues that the father word derives phonologically from 父. Neither account establishes the graph’s formation sequence or independently verified borrowing history.
The source-reported phonosemantic analysis of 爸 is not demonstrated by an inspected early inscription or sequence of dated forms of the complete graph.

limitations.text: The dossier supports a proposed 巴-to-爸 sound comparison in Zhengzhang’s system, but does not establish 巴’s original name or depicted referent; the comparison therefore cannot be confirmed from the image or independent object-name evidence.
The researched evidence reports a Three Kingdoms-era lexical attestation but does not establish a dated physical witness for the graph 爸 or the date when its components were combined.

No historical glyph image of the complete 爸 was located. The selected images are modern redraws of components, and the dossier does not support a graphic evolution sequence or a claim of corruption or replacement.
The proposed Proto-Sino-Tibetan source for the father word and the claim that 爸 preserves an older pronunciation of 父 lack independent substantiation in the dossier.
